Haiku-max single sample: the mean over the bin's puzzles of each puzzle's single-sample accuracy. Vote at k: Haiku-max's majority vote of k samples as Test B2 scores it, estimated from the samples drawn; k =
(Test B2's k). Vote of all samples drawn: the vote of all

Haiku-max samples per puzzle. A missing sample, or a sample with no answer or whose official format is not ok, votes for nothing, and a tie among several leading answers scores an equal share of one right answer when the right answer is among them (the locked vote curve's rule). Means over puzzles, in %; no intervals.
Puzzles with too few wrong samples: the puzzles in the bin with fewer than two wrong Haiku-max samples, so no agreement between wrong answers can be measured.

Wrong-sample agreement thirds (a post hoc variant of the within-bin split in Study 1's pre-specified vote lookup chart): within a bin, the puzzles with at least two wrong Haiku-max samples are ordered by how often their wrong samples give the same answer (agreeing pairs over pairs; ties broken by puzzle) and cut into a lowest, middle and highest third so that the higher thirds take any extra puzzles. Study 1's chart gives the extra puzzles to the lower thirds and sends a whole group of tied puzzles to the lower third, so these are not its thirds, and a lower third can be empty here (dashes). A bin whose puzzles all have too few wrong samples has no thirds. The rule above on which bins are read applies to bins, not to thirds: each third rests on the few puzzles in its puzzles column.
Haiku-max format compliance: the locked share of the 16-step Haiku-max samples whose official format status is ok, for all puzzles of the shape (pre-specified descriptive); it is not stamped by bin.

The unbinned rows are Study 1b's locked single-sample accuracy and vote curve (pre-specified descriptive); the post hoc recount agrees with them (checked when the table is built). Their vote at k is Test B2's challenger at that shape: Test B2 is confirmatory and pools the two shapes, so this per-shape value is a descriptive breakdown, not a test. The binned rows and the thirds are post hoc exploratory, with no causal claim.

set.printed: Study 1: the main-run puzzle set; Study 1b: its 6-step, 12-step and 16-step sets (other puzzles)

tier.printed: post hoc exploratory (no causal claim); the Study 1 Haiku-medium rows pre-specified descriptive

notes.printed: Pairs: unordered pairs of wrong samples on the same puzzle and shape. Agreeing pairs give the identical official answer (a sample with no answer or whose official format is not ok never agrees). Repeat share: agreeing pairs divided by pairs, pooled over the puzzles kept (the puzzles with at least two wrong samples).
No pairs: no puzzle had two wrong samples, so the share is undefined.

Both shapes: the chains' and the pieces' pairs and agreeing pairs added together, and the share is agreeing pairs over pairs; no count of puzzles is stamped for these rows, so Puzzles kept shows a dash.
The Study 1 Haiku-medium rows are Study 1's locked, pre-specified descriptive values; the post hoc recount gives the same counts (checked when the table is built). Every other row is post hoc.
The Study 1b Haiku-medium rows go beyond the settings this post hoc analysis was defined to cover (Haiku-max, Haiku-high and Haiku-xhigh in Study 1b, and Haiku-max on Study 1's
samples); the same post hoc recount computed them, and they are shown as the same-set medium-effort baseline for the higher efforts.

Rows differ in study, puzzle set, length and samples per puzzle; a share from few pairs or few puzzles is fragile. Setting rows side by side, above all across the two studies, is our reading, not a test.
Exploratory, no causal claim: the table does not show that repeated wrong answers cause or prevent anything.
